entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4604"/><div sID="gen6675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4604"/><hi type="bold">4. If--</hi>Rather, "Since thy children have sinned against Him, and (since) He has cast them away (Hebrew, by the hand of) for their transgressions, (yet) if thou wouldst seek unto God, &c., if thou wert pure, &c., surely [even] now He would awake for thee." Umbreit makes the apodosis to, "since thy children," &c., begin at "He has cast them away." Also, instead of "for," "He gave them up to (literally, into the hand of) their own guilt." Bildad expresses the justice of God, which Job had arraigned. Thy children have sinned; God leaves them to the consequence of their sin; most cutting to the heart of the bereaved father. <div eID="gen6675" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4611"/><div sID="gen6687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4611"/><hi type="bold">11. rush--</hi>rather, "paper-reed": The papyrus of Egypt, which was used to make garments, shoes, baskets, boats, and paper (a word derived from it). It and the flag, or bulrush, grow only in marshy places (such as are along the Nile). So the godless thrives only in external prosperity; there is in the hypocrite no inward stability; his prosperity is like the rapid growth of water plants. <div eID="gen6687" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4615"/><div sID="gen6692" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4615"/><hi type="bold">15. he shall hold it fast--</hi>implying his eager grasp, when the storm of trial comes: as the spider "holds fast" by its web; but with this difference: the light spider is sustained by that on which it rests; the godless is not by the thin web on which he rests. The expression, "Hold fast," properly applies to the spider holding his web, but is transferred to the man. Hypocrisy, like the spider's web, is fine-spun, flimsy, and woven out of its own inventions, as the spider's web out of its own bowels. An Arab proverb says, "Time destroys the well-built house, as well as the spider's web." <div eID="gen6692" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4616"/><div sID="gen6693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4616"/><hi type="bold">16. before the sun--</hi>that is, he (the godless) is green only before the sun rises; but he cannot bear its heat, and withers. So succulent plants like the gourd (<reference osisRef="Jonah.4.7">Jon 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.4.8">8</reference>). But the widespreading in the garden does not quite accord with this. Better, "in sunshine"; the sun representing the smiling fortune of the hypocrite, during which he wondrously progresses [Umbreit]. The image is that of weeds growing in rank luxuriance and spreading over even heaps of stones and walls, and then being speedily torn away. <div eID="gen6693" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4618"/><div sID="gen6695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4618"/>18. If He (God) tear him away (properly, "to tear away rapidly and violently") from his place, "then it [the place personified] shall deny him" (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.16">Psa 103:16</reference>). The very soil is ashamed of the weeds lying withered on its surface, as though it never had been connected with them. So, when the godless falls from prosperity, his nearest friends disown him. <div eID="gen6695" type="x-p"/>
